share one ChunkedSlabAllocator definition.

records.original_message_provenance:
primitives: cache PrecomputedTransactionData inside CTransaction, filled lazily

A transaction's sighash midstate (hashPrevouts, hashSequence,
hashOutputs) was recomputed each time a PrecomputedTransactionData was
built for it: in mempool acceptance and again in ConnectBlock for the
same CTransactionRef. GetTotalSize() and GetSerializeSize() also
re-walked the transaction on every call.

Store both in CTransaction:

- m_serialize_size is computed in the constructors. Serialize() with a
  SizeComputer seeks by it directly, and GetTotalSize() returns it.
- The midstate has inline storage and is filled on the first
  GetPrecomputedData() call, so transactions that are never
  script-checked (blocks loaded during assumevalid IBD, blocks read for
  reorgs or RPC, transactions only relayed) never pay for the three
  hashes. A one-byte atomic state (empty, writing, ready) publishes it
  exactly once: the fast path is a single acquire load, racing first
  callers each compute the deterministic result locally, and only the
  caller that claims the slot writes it, so the fill neither allocates
  nor races.
- PrecomputedTransactionData(const CTransaction &) copies the cache;
  CMutableTransaction still hashes, through the new
  PrecomputedTransactionData::Compute().

ConnectBlock and CheckInputsFromMempoolAndCache bind the cached data by
const reference, and MemPoolAccept no longer keeps its own copy in the
workspace.

CTransaction is shared through CTransactionRef and is now explicitly
non-copyable. Only four tests copied one; they now construct or
deserialize straight into the reference.

records.original_message_provenance:
primitives: store CTransaction around its serialization in one allocation

A CTransaction now keeps the bytes it was deserialized from (or serialized
to), and decodes its inputs and outputs next to them. Every script longer
than CScript's inline capacity borrows its bytes from that serialization,
so script bytes are stored once. Inputs, outputs and serialization share a
single allocation, and a CTransactionRef places it directly after the
shared_ptr control block, so a transaction and its reference count are one
contiguous slab slot:

  [ control block + CTransaction | CTxIn[] | CTxOut[] | serialized bytes ]

Existing code keeps reading tx.vin[i].prevout, .scriptSig and so on: the
decoded inputs and outputs are real CTxIn/CTxOut objects (only their fixed
fields duplicate the serialization), and vin/vout are spans over them.

- prevector gains a borrowed mode (indirect with capacity 0) that never
  frees or reallocates the viewed elements; copies own their elements and
  growing takes a private copy. Borrowed scripts only exist as const
  objects inside a CTransaction, so they are never modified in place.
- Deserialization reads the transaction's bytes into a per-thread scratch
  buffer, checking the structure with the same ReadCompactSize calls as
  CMutableTransaction, then allocates exactly once. Both reject the same
  truncated, trailing and non-canonical inputs.
- Serializing writes the stored bytes, and the hash is SHA256d over them,
  so neither walks the inputs and outputs again. GetTotalSize() returns
  the stored length, which replaces the cached m_serialize_size.
- Storage comes from thread-safe slabs in 128-byte size classes up to
  2 KiB, then up to 4 KiB; larger transactions use the heap.
- MakeTransactionRef builds through a TransactionRefAllocator that reserves
  the storage after the control block, and shared_ptr deserialization goes
  through a SharedPtrDeserializer hook so that block and P2P transactions
  take the same path.

Block 413567 now needs 23 heap allocations instead of 8005, and a typical
transaction none. Mempool memory accounting rises about 12% on that block
(1.75 to 1.96 MB) because the decoded inputs and outputs repeat their
fixed fields and short scripts.

another. Now the inputs, the outputs and those scripts' bytes share a
single allocation, and a CTransactionRef places it directly after the
shared_ptr control block, so a transaction and its reference count are one

inputs and outputs are real CTxIn/CTxOut objects, and vin/vout are spans
over them.

  frees or reallocates the viewed elements; copies own their elements and
  growing takes a private copy. Long scripts borrow their bytes from the
  transaction's storage. Borrowed scripts only exist as const objects
  inside a CTransaction, so they are never modified in place.
- Deserialization reads the transaction's bytes into a per-thread scratch
  buffer, checking the structure with the same ReadCompactSize calls as
  CMutableTransaction, then allocates exactly once. Both reject the same
  truncated, trailing and non-canonical inputs. The hash is computed from
  those bytes, which are not kept; the serialized size is cached for
  GetTotalSize() and SizeComputer. Serialize() writes the fields as
  SerializeTransaction does, into a per-thread buffer of exactly that
  size, and hands the stream a single write: relaying block 413567's
  transactions takes about 53 ns each instead of 127 ns with field-by-field
  stream writes.

  2 KiB, then up to 4 KiB; larger transactions use the heap.

  the storage after the control block, and shared_ptr deserialization goes
  through a SharedPtrDeserializer hook so that block and P2P transactions
  take the same path.

  (80 to 72 bytes on LP64). Serialization still writes prevout, scriptSig,

records.original_message_provenance:
primitives: build transactions from contiguous streams in place

Every deserialized CTransaction first copied its bytes into a per-thread
scratch buffer, then copied them again into its own storage. When the
stream already holds its unread bytes in one buffer, as DataStream does for
P2P messages and SpanReader does for in-memory blocks, the first copy is
unnecessary.

For such streams, ScanTransactionWire checks the transaction's structure
where it lies, with the same ReadCompactSize calls and limits as
ReadTransactionWire, and the transaction is built from those bytes. The
stream is advanced only after the transaction has been built, because
DataStream::ignore releases its buffer when it reaches the end. Other
streams (files, hashing readers) keep the scratch-buffer path.

SpanReader gains data() and ignore(), matching DataStream, so it takes
this path as well.

Block 413567 deserializes about 6% faster with software SHA-256 (about
150 us of 2.5 ms per block); the saving does not depend on hashing.

the same truncated, trailing, non-canonical and oversized inputs as
CMutableTransaction; contiguous streams leave the scratch buffer
untouched, consume exactly the transaction, and the result does not
refer to the stream's bytes.

blockstorage: read blocks into memory before deserializing them

ReadBlock deserialized straight from the block file, so every field went
through a separate buffered file read, and every transaction was copied
through the per-thread scratch buffer.

Read the block with ReadRawBlock, which checks the disk magic and size
and reads the block with one read, then deserialize it from that buffer.
Its transactions are then built in place from the buffer.

ReadBlockBench drops from about 3.17 ms to 2.43 ms (-23%) with software
SHA-256. ReadBlock now also rejects a block whose disk magic does not
match, as ReadRawBlock already did.

crypto: add ARMv8 SHA-256 instructions to the SHA-256 implementations

On arm64 SHA256AutoDetect only had the portable implementation, so every
hash on Apple silicon and ARM servers (transaction ids, merkle roots,
sighash midstates) ran in software.

Port Bitcoin Core's ARMv8 SHA-256 implementation,
src/crypto/sha256_arm_shani.cpp from bitcoin/bitcoin
924f4c4ac78b0cd3b917c694f42c0651a6f3003a (originally added by Pavol
Rusnak in 48a72fa81f, based on Jeffrey Walton's public-domain
SHA-Intrinsics, with Pieter Wuille's 64-byte two-way variant). Only its
formatting is changed, to match clang-format here.

the compiler supports the instructions (-march=armv8-a+crypto), and
selected at runtime when the CPU reports them: AT_HWCAP/AT_HWCAP2 on Linux,
hw.optional.arm.FEAT_SHA256 on macOS. The existing self-test checks it
before use.

records.subject: bench: add transaction serialization and lifetime benchmarks
records.h_provenance_message:
bench: add transaction serialization and lifetime benchmarks

Transactions are created on network threads, serialized again for every
peer they are relayed to, and often released on a different thread than
the one that created them. No benchmark covered these paths.

Using the transactions of block 413567:

- SerializeBlockTransactions serializes each one into a reused
  DataStream, as relaying them does.
- DeserializeTransactionRefs deserializes each one into a CTransactionRef
  and releases it on the same thread.
- DeserializeTransactionRefsReleasedElsewhere does the same but hands each
  reference to another thread, which releases it, through a lock-free
  single-producer single-consumer ring, so allocation and release happen
  on different threads.

With -chronik, the RPC port now also serves Chronik under /chronik
(-chronikpubliconrpcport, default 1), so a single port can carry JSON-RPC,

/wallet/ keep the ACL and Basic auth. Builds without Chronik, -chronik=0
or -chronikpubliconrpcport=0 return 404 for /chronik.

records.original_message_provenance:
http: move reply bodies into the response instead of copying them

HTTPRequest::WriteReply() took the body by const reference and copied it
into the Beast response; it now takes it by value and moves it, and the
response is moved on to the socket write. Existing callers still compile
unchanged (lvalues are copied as before); the JSON-RPC reply and the REST
block/tx/header/UTXO replies now pass rvalues, so their bodies are never
copied after being generated.

This saves one reply-sized allocation and copy per request (3.35 MB for
getblock verbosity 2 of a 1000-transaction block). Throughput on that
workload is unchanged within run-to-run noise, as JSON generation
dominates; the benefit is lower peak memory under concurrent large
replies.

records.original_message_provenance:
http: cut per-request I/O overhead (write fast path, one idle timer)

Single-connection RPC latency was 15-40 us higher than with evhttp
(e.g. a 50-call batch: 150 vs 111 us p50). Per-stage timing showed the
Beast path spending ~13 us writing a 0.7 KB reply and re-arming stream
timers on every read and write.

- WriteResponse(): on plain TCP, write directly while the non-blocking
  socket accepts data, and fall back to async_write (continuing the same
  serializer) only if it would block. Most replies now cost one writev
  and no trip through the I/O scheduler; large replies and slow clients
  still take the async path, so I/O threads never block.
- -rpcservertimeout: replace per-operation tcp_stream expiries with one
  watchdog timer per connection that wakes about once per timeout and
  shuts the socket down if the connection made no progress for that long
  while no handler (or WebSocket session) was running. Semantics are
  unchanged: idle and keep-alive connections close after the timeout,
  long-polling handlers and /p2p/ws sessions are not cut off.

c=1 p50 after (macOS arm64, loaded host): batch 130 us vs evhttp
113-119 us (was ~40 us behind), getblockcount 48-51 us vs 36-40 us (was
~20 us behind). The remaining gap is the two cross-thread handoffs.
Concurrent throughput is unchanged or better.

port, and behind a reverse proxy every request arrives from localhost and

listeners on the same server that serve only the public endpoints
(/p2p/ws, /chronik and /chronik/ws when enabled) to any client, with TLS
auto-detection and zstd as on the RPC port. JSON-RPC, /wallet/, /rest/
and every other path get 404 there regardless of client address or
credentials. This is the port to expose or point a proxy at; the RPC
port can stay on loopback.

are served only to -rpcallowip clients, like everything else there.

wallet and REST over http and https (with valid credentials, from
localhost), matches prefixes exactly, and carries node-to-node P2P over
both wss:// and plain ws:// plus an independent ws:// peer; the Chronik
proxy test covers /chronik and /chronik/ws on a public listener.
WebSocket tests start the dialed node first, so a too-early -addnode
attempt cannot leave them waiting for the slow retry.

records.h_provenance_message:
net: never self-advertise a WebSocket port as a TCP P2P address

GetLocalAddrForPeer() may adopt the address a peer reports seeing us at.

records.original_message_provenance:
net: let Sock implementations buffer data in user space

A socket implementation that decodes or decrypts in user space (TLS,
WebSocket framing) can hold received bytes that poll() cannot see, and can
accept data from Send() that it has not written yet. Add three Sock hooks,
with defaults describing a plain socket:

- HasBufferedRecv(): Recv() can return data now. CConnman then polls with
  a zero timeout and treats the socket as readable.
- PendingEvents(): OS socket events needed to flush data accepted by
  Send() (a TLS write can need RECV). CConnman polls for them even when it
  has nothing queued itself.
- FlushPending(): called when one of those events occurs; failure
  disconnects the peer.

Receiving still honours fPauseRecv when RECV was only polled on behalf of
a pending flush. Plain sockets behave exactly as before.

records.subject: net: add WebSocketSock, a WebSocket-framed P2P socket for CConnman
records.h_provenance_message:
net: add WebSocketSock, a WebSocket-framed P2P socket for CConnman

Groundwork for carrying /p2p/ws peers on the real TCP socket instead of
the socketpair bridge (an extra thread hop per side and direction, about
77 us per round trip on loopback). Not used yet.

- WebSocketCodec: RFC 6455 framing without I/O. Each P2P chunk becomes one
  binary message, zstd-compressed per the negotiated mode (p2p-zstd-v1,
  p2p-zstd, none) using P2PZstdSession. Decoding handles fragmentation,
  answers pings and closes, and rejects text frames, reserved bits and
  opcodes, wrong masking for the role, fragmented or long control frames,
  frames or messages over 64 MiB (checked from the header, before
  buffering), corrupt zstd and decompression beyond the same limit.
- WebSocketSock: a Sock CConnman polls directly. Send() frames and
  compresses on the calling thread, coalescing MSG_MORE chunks into one
  message, accepts what it is given unless more than 4 MiB is already
  waiting (then EAGAIN), and leaves the unwritten tail to the Sock
  PendingEvents()/FlushPending() hooks. Recv() deframes and decompresses;
  decoded bytes not yet returned, EOF and errors are reported through
  HasBufferedRecv(). The socket is made non-blocking (MSG_DONTWAIT may be
  defined as 0) and SIGPIPE-safe. A pluggable byte layer (plain here)
  lets TLS reuse the framing.

Unit tests cover every frame-length class in all compression modes in
both directions (incl. 3 MB payloads), MSG_MORE coalescing, buffered-data
signalling, fragmented messages with an interleaved ping, close handling,
each protocol violation, EOF mid-frame, corrupt zstd and back-pressure.
A websocket_codec fuzz target checks arbitrary input and encode/decode
round trips across arbitrary splits.

cannot be handed to CConnman. TlsByteLayer instead drives an OpenSSL
session bound to the socket itself (SSL_set_fd), non-blocking, under

- SSL_ERROR_WANT_READ/WANT_WRITE map to EAGAIN; the event a blocked write
  waits for (RECV for e.g. a TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate) is reported through
  PendingEvents(), and SSL_pending() through HasBufferedRecv().
- close_notify reads as EOF; destruction sends one non-blocking
  close_notify after the WebSocket Close.

caller-owned non-blocking sockets (partial writes, moving write buffers,
no compression or renegotiation, SSL_OP_ENABLE_KTLS where available, so
on Linux OpenSSL can offload records to the kernel), PEM loading,
self-signed certificate generation (moved from httpserver.cpp, unchanged
output), SPKI and certificate fingerprints.

both ways with and without compression, a TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate mid-stream,

  it; no local DNS lookup) when -proxy applies, the -onion proxy for
  .onion hosts, otherwise every resolved address in turn via
  ConnectDirectly(). A failed proxy never falls back to a direct
  connection, and -onlynet must include wss (onion for .onion). This
  replaces the previous refusal of WebSocket dials under -proxy.
- The dialer hook (net_websocket.cpp) then performs, synchronously on that
  socket with a 20 s deadline: TLS for wss:// with OpenSSL on the socket
  (SNI for names), and the RFC 6455 upgrade written by hand (random
  Sec-WebSocket-Key, Sec-WebSocket-Accept verified, the selected
  sub-protocol must be one we offered, extensions refused). The result is
  a WebSocketSock that CNode uses directly; leftover bytes after the 101
  response are kept.
- permessage-deflate is no longer offered outbound (node-to-node uses
  zstd); it remains accepted from inbound generic clients. The default
  -p2pwebsocketoffer is now "p2p-zstd-v1,p2p-zstd".

p2p_websocket_proxy.py uses a forwarding SOCKS5 proxy: wss:// and ws://
peers connect through it with the host name in the CONNECT request, a
dead proxy leaves no direct connection, -onlynet without wss refuses the
dial, and without a proxy the dial is direct.

records.subject: http: terminate TLS with our own OpenSSL session instead of asio's ssl_stream
records.h_provenance_message:
http: terminate TLS with our own OpenSSL session instead of asio's ssl_stream

asio's ssl::stream keeps the TLS session in its own memory BIOs, so an
upgraded connection cannot be handed elsewhere with its session. The HTTP
server now owns the TLS session itself; Beast still does all HTTP and
WebSocket parsing and serialization on top:

- TLS is detected from the first byte (0x16) peeked with MSG_PEEK, so no
  bytes are consumed; an SSL is created from the tls_util context and bound
  to the socket with SSL_set_fd.
- OsslStream is an asio AsyncStream (and non-blocking SyncWriteStream) over
  that SSL: WANT_READ/WANT_WRITE wait with async_wait, immediate results
  are re-posted (never completed inline from initiation), multi-buffer
  writes (HTTP header + body) are gathered into one SSL_write so a reply is
  one TLS record and syscall, and a write OpenSSL asked to retry is retried
  with the same length. Beast WebSocket teardown is provided for it.
- WriteResponse's non-blocking write fast path now covers TLS too.
- Until the TLS handshake completes, a deadline (-rpcservertimeout) shuts
  the socket down, so silent or stalled clients are dropped.
- -tlscert/-tlskey/-tlsephemeral and -tlsmutual behave as before;
  boost/asio/ssl is no longer used by the server.

Measured on loopback (16 RPC threads): small RPCs over TLS 45-67k req/s
at c=16/64 (plain 60-72k) and equal c=1 latency; 3.35 MB getblock replies
over TLS within noise of plain. A unit test covers handshake, reads,
gathered writes through would_block and async retry, and close_notify.

records.subject: http: hand /p2p/ws connections to CConnman without a bridge
records.h_provenance_message:
http: hand /p2p/ws connections to CConnman without a bridge

After Beast accepts a /p2p/ws upgrade negotiating p2p-zstd-v1, p2p-zstd
or no compression, the HTTP server now hands the connection itself to the
P2P layer: the TCP socket, our TLS session (wss://), and any bytes the
client sent after the upgrade request become a WebSocketSock that CConnman
polls directly. The connection leaves the HTTP server's tracking, so
stopping the HTTP server never closes P2P sockets, and P2P data no longer
crosses the HTTP I/O threads or a socketpair.

The socketpair bridge remains only for clients that negotiate RFC 7692
permessage-deflate (generic WebSocket clients) and behind the new debug
option -p2pwebsocketbridge; on platforms without local sockets
(Windows) permessage-deflate is declined and the direct path is used.

Loopback median P2P ping round trip, 3 runs (TCP 110-118 us):
  ws://, no compression   112-123 us   (was +77 us over TCP via bridge)
  ws://, p2p-zstd-v1      130-138 us
  wss://, p2p-zstd-v1     156-169 us   (bridge: 220-226 us)
The remaining difference to TCP is zstd per message and TLS.

p2p_websocket_inbound.py also covers the debug bridge; its WebSocket
client helper treats the node's Close frame as end of stream.

Integration adaptation relative to HTTP/WS series-20261019/0016: use the existing HTTPConnectionInfo::connection_id for handoff deregistration and coroutine dispatch rather than adding a second conn_id field. Reuse the existing public_only field; socket ownership and all source handoff behavior remain unchanged.

records.subject: net: pin wss:// peer keys (SPKI SHA-256)
records.h_provenance_message:
net: pin wss:// peer keys (SPKI SHA-256)

A wss:// URL may carry `#spki=<base64url SHA-256 of the peer's DER
SubjectPublicKeyInfo>`, and -p2pwebsocketpin=<host>=<spki> (repeatable)
pins every dial of a host. A URL pin takes precedence over a configured
one. After the TLS handshake the dialer compares the peer's key in
constant time and refuses a mismatch; a pin on ws:// is refused. The pin
names the key, not the certificate, so it survives re-issuing the
certificate for the same key.

getpeerinfo reports the peer's key (websocket.peer_spki, inbound peers
with a client certificate included) and whether it was pinned.

records.subject: net: size zstd output to the message, not the stream buffer
records.h_provenance_message:
net: size zstd output to the message, not the stream buffer

CompressFrame resized its output to ZSTD_CStreamOutSize() (128 KiB) plus
the bound for every message. Resizing zero-fills, so each small P2P
message paid for 128 KiB of memset: 1.1 us per 32-250 byte message, now

records.subject: net: grant inbound WebSocket peers permissions by TLS key
records.h_provenance_message:
net: grant inbound WebSocket peers permissions by TLS key

-p2pwebsocketpeer=[permissions@]<pin> recognizes an inbound P2P WebSocket
peer presenting a TLS client certificate with that public key (base64url
SHA-256 of the SPKI) and grants it permissions, with -whitelist syntax and
defaults. Setting it requests client certificates (as -tlsmutual), and
accepts any certificate: the key, not a CA, identifies the peer.

-p2pwebsocketrequirecert drops inbound WebSocket peers whose key is not
listed (including ws:// peers, which have no certificate). Plain TCP
peers are not affected. getpeerinfo's websocket.pinned reports a matched
key for inbound peers.

records.subject: http: wait for the socket to take close_notify
records.h_provenance_message:
http: wait for the socket to take close_notify

After the last HTTPS response the server made one non-blocking
SSL_shutdown. With the send buffer still full of response data that
attempt fails and no close_notify is sent: the client sees a bare FIN,
a truncated close. OsslStream::async_shutdown waits for writability
like the other operations, bounded by a 5 s deadline.

Found as a hang of ossl_stream_reads_gathers_and_retries on Linux,
whose client waits for close_notify after draining 3 MiB through a
16 KiB send buffer.

records.subject: http: neutral generated certificates and live -tlscert reload
records.h_provenance_message:
http: neutral generated certificates and live -tlscert reload

The generated datadir certificate named "bitcoind node" and localhost
for 10 years, which identifies a node to anyone who connects. It is now
issued for the first -externaldomain (else a random host name, kept
across restarts), valid for 90 days like an ACME certificate, and
renewed when fewer than 30 days remain (checked at startup and hourly).
Renewals keep the key, so SPKI pins (#spki=, -p2pwebsocketpin,
-p2pwebsocketpeer) stay valid. An existing "bitcoind node" certificate
is reissued under a neutral name for the same key.

-tlscert/-tlskey are rechecked (at most once a second, on new TLS
connections) and reloaded when replaced, e.g. by an ACME client: new
handshakes use the new certificate, existing sessions keep theirs, and a
file that fails to load keeps the previous one.

The global TLS and acceptor mutexes become GlobalMutex, as upstream
does for globals, which silences the thread-safety negative-capability
warnings.

records.subject: net,http: ALPN, SNI and a browser-like TLS client profile
records.h_provenance_message:
net,http: ALPN, SNI and a browser-like TLS client profile

To look like ordinary HTTPS on the wire:
- Servers select ALPN http/1.1 when offered, and continue without ALPN
  otherwise (h2-only clients), as HTTP/1.1 web servers do.
- The dialer offers ALPN http/1.1, and orders TLS 1.3 suites, TLS 1.2
  ciphers, groups (X25519MLKEM768 where OpenSSL >= 3.5) and signature
  algorithms like Chrome. OpenSSL cannot send GREASE values, randomize
  extension order or do ECH, so JA3/JA4 still differ from a browser.
- SNI is sent for host names, as before; dialing wss://<ip> now logs that
  TLS without a server name is unusual for web traffic.

getpeerinfo reports the agreed protocol as websocket.alpn.

records.subject: test: fix TLS unit tests and the proxy test on Linux
records.h_provenance_message:
test: fix TLS unit tests and the proxy test on Linux

- OpenSSL's socket BIO writes with write(), which raises SIGPIPE on Linux
  once the peer has closed (macOS sockets here set SO_NOSIGPIPE). The node
  ignores SIGPIPE in AppInitBasicSetup; the TLS unit test suites now do
  too, instead of being killed when one end closes before the other.
- The test SOCKS5 proxy stopped with close() only. On Linux that neither
  wakes the thread blocked in accept() nor stops the socket listening, so
  the "dead proxy" kept forwarding; shut it down first.

records.subject: http: configurable P2P WebSocket path and upgrade token
records.h_provenance_message:
http: configurable P2P WebSocket path and upgrade token

-p2pwebsocketpath serves P2P WebSocket upgrades at a path other than
/p2p/ws, and -p2pwebsockettoken (repeatable) requires a token, as
"Authorization: Bearer <t>" or a "t=<t>" cookie, compared as SHA-256
digests in constant time. With a token set, a request without one (or
with a wrong one, or not an upgrade) is handled exactly as a request for
an unknown path: the endpoint is not public, and probing it gets the same
answer as any other missing page.

Dialers take the token from wss://host/path?token=<t>, remove it from the
request target and send it as a header; logs show the URL with
token=***. Such a node is a private bridge: -externaldomain cannot be
combined with either option, since peers learning a NET_WSS address dial
/p2p/ws without a token.

records.subject: http: hand unserved public requests to a fallback web site
records.h_provenance_message:
http: hand unserved public requests to a fallback web site

-publicfallback=<host>:<port> makes -publicbind listeners look like an
ordinary web site. Any request the node does not serve there (anything
but an accepted P2P WebSocket upgrade or Chronik: pages, active probes,
upgrades with a wrong path or token) is decided on its header and handed
to that plain-HTTP server: the header as received (field names and order
kept, plus X-Forwarded-For/-Proto), anything already buffered after it,
then raw bytes both ways for the rest of the connection. Visitors and
probes get the site's responses byte for byte, over the node's TLS.

A body is never buffered by the node first, and an unreachable site gets
a bare 502. Without the option, such requests still get 404.

records.subject: args: hide URL upgrade tokens in logged arguments
records.h_provenance_message:
args: hide URL upgrade tokens in logged arguments

Startup logs every argument, so -connect=wss://host/path?token=<t> wrote
the token to debug.log. Values now show token=*** (the dedicated
-p2pwebsockettoken is already SENSITIVE). Found by the privacy recipes
